#### Accuracy and completeness — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** Why exactly-once is two guarantees — as three delivery lists built by one function and summed by another.

`deliver(mode)` produces the list of record ids a stage actually receives: 9 ids for exactly-once, 5 for at-most-once (the replay never happens), and 13 for at-least-once (the replay is not deduplicated).

`aggregate(ids)` then sums them, and step 3 is the point: it is **identical and correct** for all three lists and produces 23, 45 and 67. The duplicates are visible in the list and invisible in the number.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-meaning-memory/ch05-meaning-memory.svg" alt="Accuracy and completeness — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — at-most-once DROPS everything after the checkpoint</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-meaning-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: at-most-once DROPS everything after the checkpoint" width="980">

`indexOf(EVENTS[5])` is 5, which is > CHK = 4, so the record is skipped. All 4 records after the checkpoint are dropped and the list holds 5 ids. That is a COMPLETENESS failure: the sum will be 23, and nothing downstream can recover it.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — at-least-once APPENDS them a second time</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-meaning-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: at-least-once APPENDS them a second time" width="980">

The replayed ids are appended, so `out` holds 13 entries for 9 records — ids 5, 6, 7, 8 appear twice. That is an ACCURACY failure, and note the list itself is the evidence: the duplicates are visible here and invisible in the sum.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — and the aggregate cannot tell the two apart</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-meaning-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: and the aggregate cannot tell the two apart" width="980">

`aggregate` adds `EVENTS[id].v` for each entry and has no idea whether an id appeared before. 23, 45, 67 — three numbers from one dataset, and the function that produced them is identical and correct in all three cases.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — one duplicate costs v / window total, so thin windows hurt</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-meaning-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: one duplicate costs v / window total, so thin windows hurt" width="980">

For id 8: `base` is 8 and `v` is 8, so the cost is 100%. For id 5 the same calculation gives 14%, because its window is thicker. The duplicate is identical; only the denominator differs — which is why duplicate damage concentrates where the data is thin.

</details>

<sub>All three totals and every per-window duplicate cost are computed from the seed and asserted. Generated by `node tools/gen_ch05.js` on `tools/memkit.js`.</sub>
